10888-arthur-hamilton-and-his-dog:
Arthur Hamilton and His Dog, written for the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society and approved in 1851, is a Sunday school tale of a boy and his pet. One October evening Arthur plays before his family's small brown cottage with his brother James and a large spotted dog. Rover bows on his hind legs, tosses bread off his nose, begs with imploring paws, and barks his thanks.

The story follows Arthur leaving home, with Rover as companion and moral teacher. Its lessons are gentle: kindness, obedience, and faith in daily life. Children get a simple, affectionate tale, in the earnest style of mid-century Sunday books.
14375-the-adventures-of-grandfather-frog:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote this 1920 bedtime book about Grandfather Frog of the Smiling Pool, with pictures by Harrison Cady. The old frog, proud of his big mouth and fine voice, keeps getting into scrapes.

Longlegs the heron hunts him, Billy Mink and Little Joe Otter stir up trouble, and Spotty the turtle comes to his rescue more than once. Each short chapter ends with a gentle lesson on patience, vanity, or care. The pond setting returns in Burgess's later animal books. Burgess fills the pond with animal neighbors, and the book remains a mild, charming read for young children.
16051-the-voice-in-the-fog:
Harold MacGrath's 1915 mystery opens in a London fog so thick and yellow that eyes fail and only touch can be trusted. The book, illustrated by A. B. Wenzell and dedicated to a Florentine friend, stars Kitty Killigrew, whose portrait fronts the volume. Fog itself is almost a character, hiding streets, faces, and motives in its solid gloom.

From that murk grows a tale of voices heard but not seen, secrets, and danger in Edwardian London. MacGrath, known for The Man on the Box, writes popular romance and mystery at a swift pace. Readers who like atmosphere, intrigue, and a heroine in peril will find this a moody, entertaining thriller.
16905-the-great-red-frog:
M. Yendis, an anagram for Sidney Ransom, told and pictured this 1903 children's book, issued by Methuen in London. It opens with a little prince who looks exactly like the Lord Chamberlain's son, so alike that even the old Chamberlain at times cannot tell them apart. When the prince becomes king of Noware, the pair play in a garden where a magic bush grows up behind them.

Yendis, best known for advertising posters, made this rare children's book with pictures to match the tale. Twins, magic, and a red frog drive a short, whimsical plot. Young readers get a charming, old-style fairy tale, and collectors prize it as a scarce example of a poster artist turning to storybook work.
17102-an-elegy-on-the-death-of-a-mad-dog:
Oliver Goldsmith's comic elegy, pictured by R. Caldecott in this picture-book form, tells of a good man of Islington and the dog that bit him. Neighbors rush in, sure the dog is mad and the man is doomed. The joke lands in the last turn, when the tale flips who suffers and who survives, and the crowd's sure talk looks foolish.

Short sung stanzas, one to a page, make the piece easy to read aloud, and Caldecott's drawings carry the humor step by step. The book suits young readers and adults who like verse jokes. It is a small classic of English wit: kind to its hero, sharp on gossip, and neat in its surprise end.
17742-navajo-weavers-third-annual-report:
Washington Matthews, a doctor in the United States Army, wrote this study of Navajo weavers. It appeared in the third annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology to the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, covering 1881 to 1882. It was printed in Washington in 1884, pages 371 to 392. Plates show a Navajo woman spinning and the weaving of textiles in progress.

Readers learn how Navajo blankets and rugs were spun, dyed, and woven, with attention to tools, patterns, and work. Matthews writes as a careful government ethnologist, close to his material. The paper remains a classic source for Navajo weaving and for Southwestern material culture.
18214-our-friend-the-dog:
Maurice Maeterlinck, author of The Life of the Bee, wrote this short book on dogs, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and illustrated by Cecil Alden. The New York edition appeared in 1913 from Dodd, Mead. Maeterlinck opens with a loss: within a few days he has lost a little bulldog, only six months old, who had no history but a brief life of love.

The dog bore the name Pelleas, given by the friend who presented him. Maeterlinck describes his bulging forehead, like that of Socrates or Verlaine. He notes the blunt black nose and the hanging chops. He calls the dog beautiful after the manner of a natural monster true to its kind. Readers get a meditation on the bond between people and dogs, written by a poet who watched one small life with close, tender attention.
22750-rags-the-story-of-a-dog:
Karen Niemann wrote Rags: The Story of a Dog, a children's story told around a little boy, his grandmother, and the dog of the title. The catalog record gives no year. Animal stories for the young were a staple of the era, teaching kindness through a pet's fortunes.

The sample finds Gary building a playhouse from boxes of his own. Once the wood is carried in and the walks are swept, he calls out that everything is done. Then he asks his grandmother if he may play in the box house now. Chores first, then play, is the story's gentle economy, with Rags at the center of the household's affections. The book offers young readers a warm, simple tale of a dog and the family that loves him.
22842-the-widow-s-dog:
An American visitor meets an English flower in The Widow's Dog, a sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. The narrator recalls a favorite moment with real pleasure. She showed a visiting American the humble harebell growing wild, right where her sketch is set. He had never seen the wildflower, though poetry had consecrated it in their shared language.

He placed it in his buttonhole and quoted Scott's Lady of the Lake with enthusiasm. Around that small scene, Mitford builds her tale of a widow and the dog at its center. Flowers, loyalty, and village memory intertwine in her usual manner. The piece shows her gift for finding a whole story inside an afternoon's walk and a stranger's delight.
23348-old-mother-hubbard-and-her-dog:
This picture book retells the old nursery rhyme of Mother Hubbard and her dog in short rhymed verses, each paired with a drawing. The dame goes to the cupboard to fetch her poor dog a bone, only to find it bare, and so the pair's troubles begin.

Trip after trip follows. The dame goes to the tavern for wine, to the fair for a cake, to the baker for bread, and to the undertaker for a coffin. Each time, the dog is up to some new trick on her return. The dog stands on his head, sits in a chair, plays dead, and laughs, keeping the joke fresh to the end. Small children will love the repeat pattern and the pictures, which carry as much of the fun as the words.
23360-our-new-neighbors-at-ponkapog:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich wrote this short country tale from the view of a man who watches a small house rise on the Old Bay Road, a short walk past his own. The builder, who seems to be his own architect, tends each detail with care, and the narrator looks forward to fine new neighbours.

When a young married pair moves in, the wife pretty and lady like, the husband a bit older, the narrator's interest grows. The story follows calls, walks, and small acts of help, with humour in the gap between what the watcher guesses and what the pair truly are. It is a mild tale of country manners, curiosity, and the slow growth of friendship between houses.
2393-his-dog:
Albert Payson Terhune's His Dog gathers more Sunnybank stories, this time centering on the bond between a man and his dog. The tales show dogs as workers, friends, and family, facing danger with unshowy courage. Terhune writes from his life as a breeder, and the kennel details ring true.

The collection's sentiment is sincere rather than cloying, and its best stories still touch readers. Dog lovers will find a gentle, nostalgic book. It complements the Lad and Bruce volumes. Terhune wrote for dog magazines as well as for book readers.
24590-the-tale-of-ferdinand-frog:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this children's animal tale, part of his Sleepy-Time Tales series, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. The series tells of four-footed creatures of American woods and fields for small children, and Ferdinand Frog joins Cuffy Bear, Frisky Squirrel, Tommy Fox, and Fatty Coon on its list.

One picture shows Mr. Frog bowing to Aunt Polly Woodchuck. Bailey's tale follows Ferdinand through pond and meadow, with gentle humour and short chapters suited to bedtime. Small children get a friendly frog story, told in the simple, amusing style that made Bailey's animal books favourites.
26050-a-description-of-millenium-hall-an:
Sarah Scott, writing as a gentleman on his travels, describes Millenium Hall and its country in this book based on a 1762 Newbery reprint. A traveler writes to a friend that he meant a short letter from his northern retreat, but instead sends a volume on a society found by fortunate accident. He names their home Millenium Hall, best fitted to their lives, hiding the real name lest he offend.

Histories of Lady Mary Jones, Miss Selvyn, and Miss Trentham fill the book, with characters of the inhabitants and anecdotes meant to stir humanity and love of virtue. One servant's errand ends in grief: he meets Sir Edward borne on shoulders, pale and near breathless from a mortal wound taken by rashness in attack. Scott writes of a women's community living by kindness and sense.
26616-minnie-s-pet-dog:
Mrs. Madeline Leslie published this children's book at Boston in 1864, as one of her Minnie and Her Pets volumes, alongside the parrot, cat, horse, lamb, and monkey books. Leslie dedicates the little volumes to Henry Fowle Durant Jr., hoping they will increase his love of nature and rural life. This volume gives an account of Minnie's pet dog, Tiney, with anecdotes of other dogs.

Tiney is a spaniel with long ears, black expressive eyes, and long silky hair, fond of his ease by the hearth fire. He runs errands on the lawn, plays with Fidelle, and holds the great dog Leo in awe. Chapters promise Bose and the wig and more dog tales, all told to teach kindness to animals through a child's daily life with her pets.
2735-the-golden-dog:
William Kirby wrote this Canadian romance, Le Chien d'Or, first published in the United States in 1877 without his knowledge or sanction. Kirby's prefatory note protests that weak copyright laws left him powerless to stop that edition, and this text restores his work.

The Golden Dog follows old Quebec under French rule, with merchants, soldiers, and lovers caught in rivalry and revenge. Kirby writes with local pride and historical color. The novel endures as a classic of Canadian literature, and a tale of a city built on trade and pride. Kirby's Quebec feels lived in, from market to council chamber.
30528-the-day-of-the-dog:
Andersen Horne writes a sea adventure about Carol and Bill, who limp along in the Caribbean with water in their gas and no radio contact. Carol stares glumly at the ship-to-shore transmitter, hating to sit in mid-ocean without communication, while Bill blames sun spots for transmission failing near dusk.

Bill says the portable radio directional finder always works, and Carol wants the five o'clock news and the latest on their satellite. She switches the finder to the standard broadcast channel, hoping for a signal. Horne frames a tale in which a little dog and a man, home from a strange journey, might have been heroes, if luck and courage hold.
308-three-men-in-a-boat-to-say-nothing-o:
Jerome K. Jerome claims his book's chief beauty is simple truthfulness, not style or knowledge. Three Men in a Boat, published in 1889, records a Thames boating holiday by Jerome, George, Harris, and the dog Montmorency. The preface insists the men are flesh and blood.

George weighs about twelve stone, the preface notes, and the adventures really happened, only colored a little. River mishaps, camping quarrels, and Hampton Court history fill the trip. Jerome's comic asides made the book a lasting bestseller. It remains the classic Thames holiday tale. Jerome's Thames comedy has never gone out of print since 1889.
31327-master-of-the-moondog:
Stanley Mullen's short science-fiction story, printed in Planet Stories in July 1952, follows Tod Denver and his pet moondog, Charley. Charley is a two-yard-long creature from the moons of Saturn, described as vague and luminous, with a fat yellow balloon-like head. Denver treats him with the fond exasperation of a man stuck with an idiot child, and the pair head off on a crooked route toward the Martian diggings.

Trouble starts at once, in the story's own framing, because of Charley. On a space sled crossing the Lunar Apennines in fierce heat, the moondog curls onto the instrument panel and glares at his master. The humor comes from that mismatch: a man trying to work, and a strange, stubborn beast getting in the way at every turn.
31506-the-sweet-girl-graduates-a-farce-i:
Rea Woodman's farce The Sweet Girl Graduates was published by the Eldridge Entertainment House of Franklin, Ohio, with copyright in 1902. It is written in three acts and an epilogue, and it is built for performance by young players. Woodman dedicates it to her own boys and girls, the class of 1902.

The three acts all play in the De Smythe home, on Wednesday morning, Thursday afternoon, and Friday morning in turn. Miss Maude De Smythe, the Sweet Girl herself, is secretary of the class of 1902. The epilogue moves to the dining room of Mr. and Mrs. Jack Hamilton on a Friday morning in May 1905, and ties the schoolgirl comedy off.
32300-the-dog:
The Dog, by Dinks, Mayhew, and Hutchinson, compiled, abridged, edited, and illustrated by Frank Forester, was published in New York by George E. Woodward in a complete and revised edition. It was entered in 1873. Forester, author of Field Sports, Fish and Fishing, and Horses and Horsemanship of the United States and British Provinces, offers a new edition of Dinks and Mayhew on the dog. It was largely called for, with a further addition of his own. A frontispiece shows a setter and woodcock.

Forester's preface promises the most perfect and comprehensive work on the dog in print, and the volume serves sportsmen, breeders, and owners alike. Readers get a Victorian dog book, covering breeds, field work, and care, in the era when the dog was working companion, sporting partner, and show animal at once. The original text dates from 1873, and its advice belongs to that period.
33045-the-ranidae-how-to-breed-feed-and-:
The Ranidae is a beginner's manual on breeding, feeding, and raising the edible frog, Rana esculenta, priced at one dollar. It was published by Meadow Brook Farm of Allendale, New Jersey, and copyrighted in 1905. Its contents promise to cover every detail, from information for beginners and light work for the country home to the business side, how much to invest, and when to begin. Ponds, their construction and care, and the profit in swamp lands get early chapters.

Later sections treat nests and nest building, enemies of spawn, tadpoles, and small frogs, hatching and growth, food for tadpoles and frogs, and catching the frogs themselves. The book speaks to a time when frog farming looked like a small, practical sideline for rural households. It is a plain, thorough guide, and a curious piece of agricultural history for readers interested in forgotten farm ventures.
34448-rick-and-ruddy-the-story-of-a-boy-:
Howard Garis, famed for the Uncle Wiggily bedtime stories, wrote this tale of a boy and his dog. It came out in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1920, with pictures by John Goss. The first chapter title tells the whole setup: Rick wants a dog.

The second chapter answers it: Ruddy wants a home. Once boy and dog are joined, the tales roll on through Ruddy's first hunt, Rick getting lost, and a crow named Haw-Haw. Garis writes in a warm, simple style for young readers, with one small adventure per chapter. Readers get a classic dog story of the kind that taught many children to love reading.
38114-islam-her-moral-and-spiritual-valu:
Major Arthur Glyn Leonard, a soldier who had served in Africa, wrote this study of Islam, published in London in 1909. Syed Ameer Ali, a noted Muslim scholar, lent the book a foreword. Leonard had written on the camel, on Rhodesia, and on the tribes of the Lower Niger.

The first chapter takes on what papers then called the Moslem menace. The second outlines the temperament and character of Mohammed himself. Leonard argues, as his subtitle says, on rational and mental grounds for the moral worth of the faith. Readers get a rare thing for its day: a British officer making a fair case for Islam to British readers.
38777-lad-a-dog:
Lad, A Dog is a novel about a collie by Albert Payson Terhune, published in New York by Dutton in 1919. The print history on the copyright page tells its success. Seventeen printings ran between April and December of that first year.

Lad was a real dog of Terhune's Sunnybank kennels. A photograph of him, by Lacy Van Wagenen, serves as frontispiece. The text speaks of Lady, his mate, as part of his everyday happiness, like the sunshine itself. Terhune tells Lad's loyalty, courage, and near-human sense as a string of episodes. The book made the collie a byword for devotion in American homes. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
39750-to-your-dog-and-to-my-dog:
To Your Dog and To My Dog is Lincoln Newton Kinnicutt's tribute to dogs and masters, published by Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York in December 1915. The book proved its appeal at once: a second impression followed the same month, a third in February 1916, and a fourth in April. Its motto bids the dogs live long and prosper.

Kinnicutt addresses the book as a letter to the dogs themselves. In his library, he says, he has gathered a few of the many proofs of the affection masters bear their dogs. He apologizes for the word master, since language lacks one word for the real relationship between man and dog. Its dedication holds that a man who never called a dog his friend cannot know pure friendship in full. The anthology collects verse and prose to prove it.
41386-human-nature-and-conduct-an-introd:
Human Nature and Conduct, an introduction to social psychology, by John Dewey, was printed in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1922. The book went through six printings by April 1923. Dewey dated his opening in February 1921.

The opening treats contempt for human nature, the pathology of goodness, freedom, and the value of science. Part one treats the place of habit in conduct. Its sections hold habits as social functions, habits and will, and character and conduct. Part four closes on the good of activity, holding morality a process. It treats better and worse, evolution and progress, and making others happy. Elements in freedom and capacity end the book. Thought fans get Dewey famed study of habit, impulse, and mind in society.
41690-trading-jeff-and-his-dog:
Trading Jeff and His Dog is a boys' novel by Jim Kjelgaard. Dodd, Mead published it in New York in 1956. Twelve chapters carry the story. Titles run from The Meeting to Surprise. A standard notice declares every character imaginary.

The first chapter belongs to the dog. He creeps to the edge of a farm clearing. Starved and burr-matted, he watches a white farmhouse. His ribs show through his silky fur. He might weigh a hundred and ten pounds if fed. Now he is fifteen pounds lighter. Staghound, Great Dane, and bloodhound all show in his mongrel frame. Intelligence glows in his haunted eyes. A man splitting wood holds his whole attention. The meeting of Jeff and dog begins there.
43008-around-the-yule-log:
Willis Boyd Allen wrote Yule tales and lore to read by the log's light. The book's rights date to 1898 from Boston and Chicago. Allen wrote Snowed In and Christmas at Surf Point in past works. The year's wane leads his first tale as dusk falls with snow. Round the log, hearts draw close for old tales at that hour, he says.

The shade of Christmas Present is the next tale in his list. Lijah, a Yule muse, and a cracked bell fill the front parts. Yule folk lore gets its own sourced part in the scheme. A host's Yule feast and a trip on wheels mark the mid list. A prize find, gifts, and a storm close Allen's warm set. Gay and grave mix.
43466-not-guilty-a-defence-of-the-bottom:
Not Guilty is a defence of the failures and outcasts of society by Robert Blatchford, printed in New York by Boni and Liveright in 1918. Its subtitle calls it a defence of the bottom dog. Blatchford opens with an apology: no stiff learned work for professors, but a plain book in plain English, trusting to common sense.

He pleads for people loathed, tortured, and branded as sinful and unclean. Honours and heaven, he says, go to the fortunate and strong, while the weak get curses, blows, chains, and the gallows. The condemned are fellow flesh, victims of a hard fate rather than free choosers of evil. So the book attacks the justice of the laws, the truth of the religions, and the blame laid on the fallen.
4506-lost-in-the-fog:
James De Mille wrote this boys' adventure in 1870, opening on a beautiful July morning at Grand Pre. A crowd of boys gathers on the wharf, where the tide is high and the turbid waters of Mud Creek run. Old acquaintances gather round old scenes, with a roundabout plan for a roundabout voyage, while the doctor warns and remonstrates in vain.

The voyage must be done, and the boys set out into fog, tide, and mishap. De Mille writes with humor about Nova Scotia boys, boats, and blunders. Lost in the Fog suits young readers who enjoy sailing yarns, where a simple trip turns eventful and the fog does its worst.
46793-clown-the-circus-dog:
Vimar wrote and drew this children's book, Clown the Circus Dog, translated by Nora Hills and published at Chicago in 1917; the head gives his initial only. The contents promise Clown's puppy days, his capture, his escape, his time at the circus, and the return home. The tale opens at the end of the school year, with examinations and prizes making the last days hard on teachers and children alike.

A holiday breeze blows over the budding country, and the hum of insects promises vacation fun. Among the scholars bent over their desks sits Bertha, a dark-haired girl of twelve working for her first certificate. Her days cross with the little dog's. Vimar was a French artist known for animal tales, and this one charms with pictures on nearly every page.
47563-jim-the-story-of-a-backwoods-polic:
Jim: The Story of a Backwoods Police Dog is an animal story by Charles Roberts, a major and a famed Canadian writer of wild life, copyrighted in 1918. This edition was printed in New York in 1931. Roberts helped invent the realistic animal story, told from the beast's own side.

Jim's mother is a big cross-bred bitch, half Newfoundland and half bloodhound, at the Brine's Rip Mills. With a busy master and the deep wilderness around, she runs wild and becomes a deadly hunter. Her pup Jim grows into the backwoods police dog of the title. Other tales in the book tell of an eagle, a mule, and a skunk called Stripes the Unconcerned. Roberts writes nature red in tooth and claw.
47897-the-yule-log:
A Christmas story book for the young fills this volume, The Yule Log, published at New York in 1859. Its introduction explains the old custom. On Christmas Eve an enormous log, the trunk or root of a great tree, was paraded into the house. The father bore it in his arms while the family marched after to music. It was lit with a brand saved from last year's clog.

Then the household drew about the fire with nut-brown ale, and the song and tale went round. The editor, writing at Golden Hill in November 1858, tries to snatch a brand from memory's embers for his young readers. The contents list fairy tales: the boy and his silver wings, the sparrow and the fairy, and the princess and the rose. It is a Victorian Christmas annual in miniature.
48078-history-of-embalming-and-of-prepar:
History of Embalming is a work on the preservation of the dead and of specimens for study. Its full title joins the art of embalming to preparations in anatomy and pathology. Notes by the transcriber stand at the head of the text. Paired underscores mark words in italics, and footnotes stand below the sections they bear on, the notes state.

One note gives a caveat on the book itself. The text is not a strict rendering of the first French work, it says. The author and translator left out large parts of the first book. He also put in notes and remarks of his own, without always marking them as his. The English text thus shifts from the French in many places, the note warns. The work is a history of how the dead were kept, from the age of Egypt to the dissecting room.
48861-jack-the-fire-dog:
Lily Wesselhoeft wrote this dog story for children, first copyrighted in 1903 and reprinted at Boston in 1927. Ashley drew its pictures, and Wesselhoeft had already written Sparrow the Tramp and other animal tales. A frontispiece shows a fire crew dashing out with Jack bounding ahead.

Jack lives at Engine 33, kept in a solid brick firehouse. Pictures promise rescues: a young fireman bearing a still boy from a burning house, and Jack looking with sorrowful eyes at old friends. A boy named Sam threads the tale, sharing lunches and sleigh rides with the dog. Readers get a warm period tale of the horse-drawn fire service and its mascot.
48981-dissection-of-the-platana-and-the-:
Dissection of the Platana and the Frog is a zoology laboratory manual by Gilchrist and von Bonde of the University of Cape Town. Cape Times printed it in 1919. Its preface explains why such a book was needed. Some animals available for study in South Africa differ from those in textbooks written for other countries.

Special directions and diagrams were therefore drawn up for local laboratory use. The course begins with a study of a vertebrate type. The platana, or clawed toad, serves as the most convenient type in South Africa, and in some respects the most instructive. The frog follows for comparison. The manual guided students through each cut and structure.
49243-from-dartmouth-to-the-dardanelles-:
From Dartmouth to the Dardanelles, a midshipman log, was shaped by the writer mother and first printed in London by William Heinemann in June 1916. Fresh printings came in July, September, and October of that year. The book stands in a set named Soldiers Tales of the Great War, at three shillings and sixpence.

In her foreword the mother says the blame for printing the book lies with her, and with her alone. She trusts the great Silent Service, whose finest custom is to do and not to talk, will see no indiscretion in it. The pages make no claim to literary merit, she says, being simply a boy story of ten months at sea. Many who read the log urged her to print it. War readers get a young naval cadet voyage to the Dardanelles in his own words.
49514-literature-of-the-indian-languages:
Literature of the Indian Languages is a bibliographical catalogue of books and scripture versions in the Indian tongues of the United States, printed at Washington in 1849. A gathering of such translations was then being made in the Indian Bureau of the War Office. The list was issued in part to warn translators against sending work already held, and to draw in what was missing.

Its compiler holds that the true history of the tribes rests on the light thrown by their languages. To sort the tongues into families would, he argues, restore old relations among the peoples. The catalogue opens with the Iroquois, starting with Mohawk, and gives brief critical notices of each book, grammar, and vocabulary.
55605-histoire-du-chien-de-brisquet-the-:
Histoire du chien de Brisquet, The Story of Brisquet's Dog, is a French tale by Charles Nodier (1780-1844). The e-text prints the French first, followed by an English translation. Brisquet is a woodcutter in the forest of Lions, near the hamlet of La Goupilliere. He lives poorly from his fagots with his wife Brisquette. They have two children and a dog.

Biscotin is seven and dark; Biscotine is six and fair. The dog, la Bichonne, is black all over except her fire-coloured muzzle. She is the best dog in the country for attachment to her masters. The tale turns on the year of the great snows. Wolves filled the forest, and poor people struggled to live. Brisquet warns his wife each morning to keep the children and the dog in. One evening he does not come home at the usual hour.
57028-a-dominie-s-log:
A Dominie's Log is the diary of a young Scottish schoolmaster, written by A S Neill and published by Herbert Jenkins of London. Neill also wrote A Dominie Abroad and A Dominie Dismissed. The book exists, he explains, because the official school log book forbade general reflections and opinions.

The Scottish code left the dominie needing a safety valve. So he kept a private log of the day's troubles and comedies. Sometimes his unconventionality startled even his own bairns. Much in education he admits he does not understand. The one thing he comprehends is the child mind, and he has the saving quality of humour. Neill later founded Summerhill, the famous free school. This log shows the young teacher already chafing at the code, ruler, and rote of his first classroom.
5759-the-day-of-the-dog:
George Barr McCutcheon published The Day of the Dog in New York in 1904, with illustrations by Harrison Fisher. Part one opens with Crosby planning a hurried train trip, since he has heard Mrs Delancy leaves for New York that night, and delay would bring troublesome complications. Crosby promises Graves he will join a box party that evening, then faces three hours of rank scenery each way, plus a drive into the country.

It offers a light society comedy of appointments, trains, and tangled plans, told with McCutcheon's polished ease. The novel favors witty talk and social maneuver over grand drama, as a single day's errands threaten a whole evening's pleasures. Fans of early twentieth-century popular romance will enjoy its brisk pace and its picture of fashionable life on the move.
58423-eight-girls-and-a-dog:
Eight Girls and a Dog is a girls' story by Carolyn Wells. The Century Company published it in New York in 1902. It belongs to the Saint Nicholas Books series. The contents list sixteen chapters of housekeeping adventure. PilLows and Pitchers opens the tale at page three. On the Road and The Fun Begins follow in order. The Whitecap and The Enchanted Princess give chapter titles. Hester's Dinner and an Indian caller come in the middle.

Fritters and Salad and Genius Burns continue the housekeeping frolic. The Play's the Thing and a successful performance turn theatrical. Hide-and-Seek and Willing Service fill the later chapters. A Welcome Invitation closes the list of contents. A frontispiece shows Mrs Lennox exclaiming at the girls filing in. Timmy Loo the dog is held in one illustration. Wells writes a summer of girls keeping house together.
5947-billy-bunny-and-uncle-bull-frog:
David Cory tells linked bedtime stories of Billy Bunny and Uncle Bull Frog, in a series that also includes Billy Bunny and Daddy Fox, the Friendly Elephant, and Uncle Lucky Lefthindfoot. Illustrations by Hugh Spencer accompany the tales, which proceed story by story, each ending with a promise of what comes next. One story finds the Policeman Cat arresting Billy Bunny and Uncle Lucky, raising his club to tickle a hind foot.

A big elm tree begins to bark just then, scaring the Policeman Cat nearly to death, since he mistakes it for a dog. Young readers get gentle woodland comedy, where rabbits, frogs, cats, and trees play at danger without real harm. The book suits bedtime reading aloud, with short stories, familiar animal friends, and a storyteller's voice that pauses for tomorrow.
59909-pep-the-story-of-a-brave-dog:
Clarence Hawkes wrote a dog story copyrighted in 1922, drawn by William Van Dresser and dedicated to dog lovers the world over. A front essay, A Friend to Man, opens the book. Hawkes calls it an irony of fate that man's faithful friend sprang from the wolf. The wolf, he says, is a hated and despised brute, yet the true father of the dog.

Hawkes traces how wolves hung around the campfires of cave dwelling man. Wounded and poisoned, they still could not be driven away. A picture shows Pep sniffing eagerly at his master's face. The story that follows presents Pep as a brave dog in that long line of descent.
61429-the-heart-of-a-dog:
The Heart of a Dog is a story collection by Albert Payson Terhune, illustrated by Marguerite Kirmse and published by Doubleday in 1924. Terhune's Sunnybank collies are the book's centre: the contents promise the coming of Lad, the most famous of them, Lochinvar Bobby, a tracker story, and a fox story to open. The dedication is to the only boy the conservative Sunnybank collies accepted as a playfellow.

The opening tale turns on silver foxes. Two partners found a kennel company with comfortable capital and an uncomfortable ignorance of the fox's mind. They memorized the diet charts and the government bulletin on fox farming, but knew nothing of fox mentality. Terhune's moral follows: chickens, hogs and cattle may be raised without studying their brains, but no one succeeds with foxes, or their fifth cousins the collies, without learning the mental animal. The stories that follow apply that creed to dogs.
64323-beyond-the-yellow-fog:
Beyond the Yellow Fog is a tale of the stars by Emmett McDowell. It first ran in a press sheet of world tales in the spring of nineteen forty-seven. A front blurb calls the foe of the tale the small death, a creep of yellow mist in a strange ship. Gavin Murdock, a hard man hunter, is its lead.

The tale opens as Murdock sits past a desk of glass on Mars and gives a thin count of his life. He was first mate of works on a grand liner of the star ways. He lost that post past a blow to his chiefs nose and has been stuck on a port world since. He signs on a slave ship of the far worlds, though the law of Earth strips such men of their home rights. The fog waits past that choice.
66027-the-woodcutter-s-dog:
The Woodcutter's Dog turns Charles Nodier's tale Le Chien de Brisquet into English, printed at London in 1921. Claud Lovat Fraser drew the pictures, and the foreword calls the story a favourite that has held French children for generations. Nodier's dog, in the French title, is named for its master, the woodcutter Brisquet.

Brisquet, also called the Man with the Trusty Axe, lives in the Forest of Lions near a fine well. He and his wife Brisquette are poor, living by the sale of his faggots, with two small children and a black curly dog named Bichonne. The tale is set in the year of the Great Snow, when wolves swarmed in the forest and poor folk fought to live.
67564-jerry-todd-and-the-talking-frog:
Jerry Todd and the Talking Frog is a boys' fun mystery by Leo Edwards, published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. Jerry himself opens the book with a note on the title. He had meant to call it the puzzle room mystery, but Scoop, the boys' leader, pointed out that the talking frog fills more of the book. So the frog gave the story its name.

The fun part, Jerry says, is where they peddle a spy's beauty soap, Bubbles of Beauty, which does amazing things. There is a ghost in the story too, walking the porches of an old haunted house at midnight. The boys keep the doors locked, alone in the brick house: Scoop, Peg, and their new chum Tom Ricks, whom they brave the haunting to help. His books packed chuckles and tangles for young readers of the twenties.
68868-bulldog:
Max Brand wrote this Western tale under the title 'Bulldog' in its magazine form. A plate shows Peter Zinn greeting his wife roughly, telling her to care for a pup he calls his kind of dog. Zinn comes home from prison as the story opens on the platform.

No one meets him at the station except the constable, Tom Frejus, with a hand on his shoulder. Frejus urges him to let prison be a lesson and not to beat men up for being stronger. Zinn has spent a year breaking rocks for state roads, growing harder, and nursing his old hate for Frejus all the while.
68943-the-voice-in-the-fog:
The Voice in the Fog is a sea tale by Henry Leverage. Its ship is the Seriphus, a ten thousand ton ocean tanker built on the Clyde. She carries petrol to Brazil and crude oil to Asia. Her plain round of trade routes ends when Captain Ezra Morgan takes her over.

Morgan drives the tanker into strange Eastern seas, loading oil in California. He has the daring of a Norseman and the thrift of a Maine Yankee. Below decks rules his rival, chief engineer Paul Richter, too skilled with steam to be removed. The owners like opposed forces on a ship. Leverage builds his tale on that feud, and on the side trading both men run.
69789-the-fellowship-of-the-frog:
Edgar Wallace wrote The Fellowship of the Frog, a crime novel published in London in 1926. A secret gang known as the Frogs spreads fear, led by a hidden chief called the Frog. Maitland, a rich and strange man, sits near the centre of the web. Ray, Elk, and Broad are drawn into the case, along with police raids and a broadcast.

Chapters move from Maytree Cottage to Harley Terrace and Eldor Street. A wrecked man, a morning-after scene, and sudden calls keep the pace quick. Wallace was known for fast thrillers, and this one piles clue on clue. The truth about Ray comes out as the net closes on the gang.
70037-the-fog:
The Fog is a novel by William Dudley Pelley, first printed at Boston in 1921. Pelley dedicated it to his own boy at eighteen, dating the dedication from Dandelion Farm at Passumpsic, Vermont, in June 1921. The novel is built in two books: Drizzle and Murk, and Sunshine Glorious. Its first chapters are called This Freckled World and The Dresden Doll.

The narrator remembers himself as a boy straddling a seven-foot fence at the north boundary of a Vermont school yard. It was the opening morning of the September term, and he had left home dressed in the full armour of country-village scholarship. The puckering-string of his blouse was already broken, and his new dollar-and-a-quarter boots were hot. Later chapters treat the fairy foundling, prayer, bending the twig, and first complications. The second book turns to too easy money and good resolutions.
70358-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-and:
Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue and Their Trick Dog is a children's book by Laura Lee Hope, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Walter Rogers drew the pictures, with a frontispiece of the dog Pat pulling hard. Hope wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Six Little Bunkers books as well.

Bunny and Sue are a young brother and sister whose days turn on small adventures. The tale opens near supper time, with Bunny racing to answer a call. Their trick dog stands at the center of this volume, by the title's promise. Readers in the long Bunny Brown series get gentle fun, family warmth, and a clever pet to cheer for.
71750-leaves-from-a-middy-s-log:
Arthur Lee Knight wrote Leaves from a Middy's Log, printed by Thomas Nelson and Sons in London and Edinburgh. Knight also wrote Adventures of a Midshipmite, The Rajah of Monkey Island, and The Cruise of the Cormorant. A front picture shows the young hero in agony of dread, kneeling at the side of his friend Charlie.

A middy is a midshipman, the boy officer in training in the age of sail and early steam. The log form lets Knight string sea adventures as diary leaves, with storms, foreign ports, and shipboard pranks. Boys of the day devoured such tales. Readers get a brisk naval yarn told from the lowest rung of the officer ladder.
72039-the-story-of-a-woolly-dog:
The Story of a Woolly Dog is a children's book by Laura Lee Hope. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York in 1923. Harry Smith illustrated the volume for young readers. It belongs to the Make-Believe Stories series of toy tales. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown series. The contents list ten chapters of a toy dog's adventures. Poor Toys opens the tale in a little toy shop. A Rich Man and The Woolly Dog's New Home follow. What Little Jane Did and A Lost Diamond come next.

The China Cat and In the Beehive fill the middle chapters. A Strange Discovery closes the contents. The first chapter's shopkeeper praises the dog as his finest toy. But unsold toys cannot pay the rent, she laments. Hope's toys talk and adventure when children are absent.
7281-tom-cringle-s-log:
Michael Scott's Tom Cringle's Log opens with Thomas Cringle, thirteen years old and four feet four inches, dazzled by the glories of Trafalgar in a merry month of May. He resolves that Britain shall no longer languish for want of a successor to Nelson. He sets himself to torment every man and woman connected with him until they agree to exert all their influence for his naval career.

The boy's grand resolve, told in his own comic voice, launches a sea tale of ships, storms, and West Indian life. Scott writes with a sailor's gusto and a humourist's eye for youthful swagger. Cringle's log follows a small hero with large dreams onto a very large ocean.
77560-the-anatomy-of-the-frog:
The Anatomy of the Frog is a lore book on the build of the frogs frame, for students of the life craft. Notes at its front tell how this deep book was kept in print form. Its marks, gaps, and marks of speech were held as first struck, in the main.

A list at its end tells the spell faults that were set right in this form. Its prints are of all sizes and depths, the notes warn. They have been moved to stand near the text they serve. So its list of prints gives just a rough guide to where each stands. Its parts run bone by bone, cord by cord, and gut by gut, the full map of the beast that starts most school cuts.
78757-the-sheriff-of-sun-dog:
The Sheriff of Sun Dog is a western novel by Tuttle, who had written Sun Dog Trails and Law Rustlers before it. The tale opens on a hot day in Marlin City, county seat of Sun Dog county. Folk said there was only one tree between the town and the Arctic Circle to break the north winds. It stood too far north to give shade in summer, the narrator jokes.

A forlorn horse hangs its head at the hitch rack, and a lean dog hunts a shady spot on the board walk. In the sheriff's office sit the new sheriff, Brick Davidson, and his deputy, called Silent Slade. The old sheriff had named Brick his deputy and resigned in his favour, glad to be quit of the place. Tuttle builds his west dry, funny, and sudden.
7884-in-the-fog:
Richard Harding Davis's In the Fog opens at the Grill, called the hardest club in the world to enter. Membership there rivals a Garter or a Vanity Fair cartoon. Members never name it, lest praise sound like boasting, and they still blot letters with sand.

The club dates to Shakespeare's Theatre on the Times site. It holds a golden grill from Charles II and Pierce Egan's Tom and Jerry manuscript, and has blackballed a prime minister of each party at one sitting. Through fog, supper talk, and four strangers, Davis builds a witty London mystery.
9463-the-under-dog:
F. Hopkinson Smith wrote this book of the under dog in 1903, illustrated throughout. His preface defines the term: men who lose place through weakness, lost chances, or impaired powers, and must always be under dog in the fight. Others are misjudged by fellows, or crushed by law with a sentence, while still others are misunderstood and out of touch.

Such men, Smith says, have hearts chilled by neglect, whose coals need only a warm breath of sympathy to flame again. His tales follow such figures with compassion. The book remains a humane collection, Victorian in sentiment and generous in spirit.
9478-the-dog:
William Youatt wrote The Dog in the mid-1800s, a full guide to dogs for owners, breeders, and vets of the day. E. J. Lewis, a Philadelphia doctor, edited this edition and added new matter. The book covers breeds from bloodhounds and greyhounds to spaniels, terriers, and sheep dogs, with plates of each type. It treats the dog as a working friend, not a mere pet.

Pages take up form, temper, training, kennel care, and ills of each breed, from the Newfoundland to the tiny Blenheim. Youatt draws on long practice with hounds and gun dogs, and gives plain rules for feed, work, and cure. A reader gets a rich picture of Victorian dog life, and a store of old lore on breeds that still walk our streets today.
an-elegy-on-the-death-of-a-mad-dog: Oliver Goldsmith writes an elegy on the death of a mad dog, pictured by Randolph Caldecott in one of his picture books. The short comic poem turns a village tale of a dog and its master into gentle satire. Sung and pictured for children, it keeps Goldsmith's humour alive in nursery form.
arthur-hamilton-and-his-dog: Anonymous tells a homely tale of Arthur Hamilton and his clever dog Rover, who bows, begs, and tosses bread from his nose for the boys. While children play on a cottage piazza, their mother watches with strength and Christian patience earned over hard years. The story pairs animal antics with a lesson in kindness and steady home life. It is short, sweet, and made for young readers of an earlier age.
billy-bunny-and-uncle-bull-frog: David Cory's 1920 children's book collects short tales of Billy Bunny and his animal neighbours. Billy meets Mr. Blacksnake, a freshwater crab, a sorrowful jay bird, a policeman cat, a gray mouse and Uncle Bull Frog, and tries novelties like the ting-a-ling telephone. Each brief adventure ends kindly, in the vein of Cory's other Billy Bunny volumes.
britannica-1911-cog:
Cog is a short word with three split senses, and the entry treats each in turn. The first sense names a broad, round ship used for trade and war until the 1400s. Its roots lie in Teutonic and Romance tongues, though the link between them is obscure. The English cock-boat comes from the French form of the word.

The second sense is the one still in daily use. A cog is a tooth on the rim of a wheel. Such teeth are cut in the wheel or fixed into it. They mesh with teeth on a second wheel to pass motion on. The third sense is slang for a cheat at dice. Old use shows the cheat lay in sleight of hand, not in loaded dice. The entry keeps the three apart with care.
britannica-1911-crannog:
Crannog is the name used in Scotland and Ireland for the stockaded islands built long ago in the lochs of both lands. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces how study of them grew after John Mackinlay reported two in Bute in 1813. Sir William Wilde examined the Irish crannog of Lagore in 1840, and Swiss lake finds of 1853 sped the work.

Builders raised islets or shallows with logs, brushwood, and stones, ringed them with one or two lines of stakes, and floored them with earth or flags. Huts of logs or wattles stood inside, and a log bridge, a stone causeway, or dugout canoes gave the only way ashore. Over 150 have been examined in Ireland and more than half that count in Scotland. One Ayrshire example held a paved hearth and a refuse heap beside its door.
britannica-1911-fog:
Fog is the name for solid or liquid particles spread through the surface layers of the air thickly enough to make nearby objects dim or invisible. In its strongest forms it hinders travellers by sea and land, by railway, road, river and mountain path. At its worst it can paralyse traffic altogether. The word, the entry suggests, is a back formation from foggy. That adjective came from an older fog meaning rank grass or, in northern Britain, moss, and fog clings to meadows and marshes.

Mist and haze are near relations, used in ordinary writing with little fixed difference. The long article sorts the three terms and studies the thing itself. It treats how fog forms, its kinds over land and sea, and the harm it does to travel and trade.
britannica-1911-frog:
Frog is a zoology name of wide use, strictly for animals of the family Ranidae within the tailless batrachians. The common British frog, Rana temporaria, and its allies the edible frog and the American bull-frog stand as types. The genus Rana is set out by bone and tooth marks, a forked protruding tongue, and more or less webbed toes, across about 200 species.

Those species live over nearly the whole world, missing most of South America and Australia. Some are fully aquatic, some burrow with a sharp heel spur, and some climb by disks on the toe tips. The entry warns that such habits once drove classification and misled it, since tree-frogs proper stand anatomically nearer the toads. Giants include the bull-frog at near 8 inches and Rana goliath at 10. Odd members named are the hairy frog of West Africa and the parachuting Rhacophorus of Asia.
britannica-1911-gog:
Gog is the subject of a scripture entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a Hebrew name found in the book of Ezekiel and in Revelation. It denotes a power set against God's rule that will show itself before the end. Possible roots for the name are weighed at the start.

Links to a land called Gag, to an Assyrian ruler, and to Gyges of Lydia are all put forward. In the later passage Gog and Magog stand side by side as a pair. In the earlier passage Gog is the person or people and Magog is the land they come from. The entry sorts those uses with care.
britannica-1911-hunting-dog:
Hunting Dog is a zoology article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an African wild dog. The species named in Latin in the entry differs from the rest of its family in two ways. It has only four toes on each foot, and its coat is blotched in yellow, black, and white. It is nearly as large as a mastiff.

The entry describes long limbs, a broad flat head, a short muzzle, and large upright ears. In looks it bears a passing likeness to the spotted hyena, and is sometimes called the hyena dog. These dogs live in nearly all of Africa south and east of the Sahara. They hunt in packs and do great harm to sheep flocks. A quoted hunter's claim that a pack could run down the swiftest antelope is, the article says, fully confirmed.
britannica-1911-krivoy-rog:
Krivoy Rog is a town of south Russia, in the government of Kherson, on the Ingulets River. It stands near the station of the same name on the Ekaterinoslav railway, 113 miles S.W. of the city of Ekaterinoslav. In 1900 it held about 10,000 people. The hosted text for this record is a segment inside a shared file that also holds parts of neighbouring entries; the segment is the town's own short article.

The town is the centre of a district very rich in minerals. They come from a narrow belt of crystalline schists lying under the Tertiary beds. Iron ores running 60 to 70 per cent iron are dug here, along with copper ores, colours, brown coal, graphite, slate and lithographic stone. Nearly 2,000,000 tons of iron ore are raised each year.
britannica-1911-ostrog:
Ostrog, a town in Russia in the district of Volhynia, is described in a brief 1911 Britannica article. It lies ninety five miles west of Zhitomir, where the Vilya meets the Goryn River. Its count in 1897 was 14,530 people. The town is a seat of the Orthodox Greek Church.

In past years Ostrog held a noted school of classics, later turned into a Jesuit college. The first Bible rendered into old Slavonic was made and printed there in 1581. A church brotherhood in the town runs schools of its own. Trades list leather work, pots, oil, soap, and candles. The town fell into decay after attacks in the 1600s.
britannica-1911-taganrog:
Taganrog, a seaport of southern Russia on the north shore of the Sea of Azov, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands in the Don Cossacks territory, some 170 miles from Ekaterinoslav. Built mainly of wood on a low cape, it has the look of a busy trading city. The imperial palace, where Alexander the First died in 1825, is noted. Statues of Alexander and of Peter the Great adorn the town.

Pisan merchants founded a colony there in the thirteenth century, but it soon vanished. Russia annexed the point only in 1769. Its trade dates from the second half of the nineteenth century. Rail links sped its growth, and its people reached 58,928 in 1900. Greeks, Jews, Armenians, and western Europeans form key parts of that population. An Anglo-French fleet bombarded the town in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gog-and-magog:
Gog and Magog are the names, respectively, of a king and his supposed kingdom, named several times in Ezekiel 38 and 39, and a single time in the Apocalypse. Ezekiel is commanded to set his face against Gog, the land of Magog, chief prince of Mosoch and Thubal. A Catholic Encyclopedia article weighs the vague evidence for who and where they were.

Gog's invasion host includes Persians, Ethiopians, Libyans, Gomer, and the house of Thogorma. It comes from the northern parts. Some writers read Gog as a generic figure for the enemies of Israel, or of the Church, and others as a royal title like Pharaoh. More probably both names are historical: Gog may be Gyges of Lydia, called Gu-gu on Assyrian inscriptions, though Josephus and others identify Magog with Scythia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist Alzog, a Catholic church historian born at Ohlau in 1808 and dead at Freiburg in 1878. He studied at Breslau and Bonn, was ordained in 1834, and took a Munich doctorate in 1835. After Posen in 1836, Hildesheim in 1845, he took Freiburg's church history chair in 1853 with a councillor's rank.

Alzog stoutly defended Posen's Archbishop Dunin against Prussian persecution, and later joined the Vatican preparatory commission on dogma. Amiable and virtuous in character, he wrote a Manual of Church History through nine editions to 1872 in many tongues, a Patrology through four editions. There is also an edition of Gregory Nazianzen's Apologetic Oration, besides wide periodical work.
doe-osti-17014396-firetec-bug-resolution:
Consolidated bug log for FIRETEC, a fire modeling code, covers investigations from May through September 2026 at Los Alamos National Laboratory. Colby Fronk, Jenna McDanold, Matthew Huckins, Sara Brambilla, and Alexander Josephson compiled the record, issued September 24, 2026. Each entry carries a dated bug number and a plain statement of the fault found.

Early entries deal with pressure gradient scaling, boundary updates, and heat source controls that acted globally instead of per source. Other entries cover terrain depth handling, fragile input reading, and math checks that could divide by zero. The log pairs each fault with its fix, so code users can trace what changed and why across the season.
doe-osti-2571040-evonet-a-phylogenomic-a:
Final report DE-SC0014377, led by Gloria Coruzzi of New York University with co-investigators at seven partner institutions, covers the EvoNet project from 2015 through a no-cost extension to 2024. The team hunted for genes that let plants survive in the nitrogen-poor soils of Chile's Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth. Their finds are meant as targets for hardier crops and biofuel grasses.

Collectors focused on 32 Atacama extremophile species, including seven grasses with biofuel promise. Each was matched with close sister species from nitrogen-rich arid and mesic parts of California. Deep RNA sequencing and fresh transcriptome assembly fed a phylogenomic search for genes under positive selection. The project also released a database of selected gene groups, a metabolomics data set, and a public pipeline called PhyloGeneious for this kind of evolutionary comparison.
doe-osti-2571553-interactions-between-ae:
Final technical report DE-SC0020056, led by Edward Z. Zipser with Zhixiao Zhang, James Russell, and Peter Veals, uses data from the CACTI field campaign in Argentina. Instruments deployed for the 2018 to 2019 campaign watched thunderstorms erupt almost daily over the same mountain range. The team asked whether airborne particles, dust and smoke, make those storms stronger, as many earlier studies had suggested.

After weather factors were accounted for, the answer ran the other way. Storm depth tracked meteorology closely, especially the level of neutral buoyancy and deep wind shear. Once those links were removed, higher particle counts mostly went with warmer cloud tops, meaning shallower storm cores. A side effort ran a six-and-a-half-month storm-resolving simulation of mesoscale storm systems. It matched observed life cycles well, though its rain areas ran small and its systems moved too fast.
doe-osti-2999893-the-ai-base-nda-catalog:
Megan Booher, Tyler Nagel, Rollin Lakis and Robert Weinmann-Smith present a reference catalog in LA-UR-25-30540, issued 23 October 2025, from Los Alamos National Laboratory. NDA, nondestructive assay, measures nuclear material without opening or consuming it, the only practical way to inventory guarded stock. Choosing the right assay for each material is a specialist skill. This catalog pairs material descriptions with the measurement method that fits them best, and explains why.

Each entry gives a clear recommendation with supporting detail. For plutonium carrying americium salt impurities, for instance, it prescribes high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy with an HPGe detector and isotopic software such as FRAM. The americium isotope americium-241 shouts a strong 59.5-kiloelectronvolt gamma ray that can swamp the plutonium signal, so filters and careful background handling are spelled out. Calibration against like-shaped standards is advised throughout. The catalog aims to put expert first choices in reach of newer staff.
doe-osti-3003183-packages-of-distributed:
Cindy Zhu and Cynthia Regnier of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory survey demonstration projects in a November 2025 report. The projects bundle distributed energy technologies: rooftop solar, batteries, smart thermostats, and flexible loads. The point is demand flexibility at community scale, shifting when whole neighborhoods draw power so the grid is stressed less at peaks.

Teams across the country chose their technology packages in different ways. Some modeled first, some ran cost-benefit frameworks with utilities or local stakeholders, and some simply piloted widely to learn. The report organizes packages by building type: multifamily, single-family, commercial, and campus. One project targets deep retrofits in disadvantaged communities in Seattle and New York City. Trends across the projects show which technologies survived cuts and which grid services they delivered.
doe-osti-3014667-security-of-ders-and-gr:
Danish Saleem of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory presented this slide deck, dated July 9, 2025. Its topic is the security of distributed energy resources and grid edge technologies. Rooftop solar, batteries, smart inverters, and virtual power plants now sit at the grid's edge. Many parties own them. The deck frames that shift as a new frontier. It is more distributed, intelligent, and complex. Its risks are not yet well understood.

A stakeholder map spans manufacturers such as Tesla, Enphase, and SolarEdge. It also spans utilities, aggregators, test laboratories, and regulators. A timeline traces DER cybersecurity standards work from 2004 toward anticipated releases through 2028. The IEEE 1547 interconnection series anchors it. The presentation argues the industry still lacks a shared approach. Devices that utilities do not own, but must rely on, need that shared approach.
doe-osti-3018361-advanced-mixed-mode-com:
Michael Hughes of GE Vernova led this final report for cooperative agreement DE-FE0032173, submitted February 17, 2026. The project ran from October 2022 until the department terminated it on October 10, 2025. Its goal was a retrofittable combustor module for the frame 7F gas turbine, letting plants burn hydrogen blended into natural gas at any ratio from zero to one hundred percent.

Performance targets were strict. The package had to keep current cycle performance while holding nitrogen oxide emissions at the equivalent of 25 parts per million, dry, corrected to fifteen percent oxygen. Axial fuel staging was expected to stretch compliant turndown below twenty percent of full load. Budget period three was cancelled by the termination. Test sections record the final hardware state, including injector response measurements near background noise for the first three injectors. Turbine owners planning hydrogen conversions inherit the design record and its limits.
doe-osti-3019695-development-of-pnnl-s-p:
Jacqueline Royer, Matthew Athon, Dallin Barton, and six colleagues built a plutonium metallography capability at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, documented in this January 2026 report. Metallography reads a metal's history in its microstructure: grain shapes, phases, and inclusions. Plutonium makes that reading hard, since samples are radioactive and the metal itself is chemically restless. The report describes the preparation and imaging work inside the lab's controls. Images from backscattered electron detectors compare alpha-phase and delta-phase plutonium samples.

The alpha samples carried a much higher volume fraction of globular and faceted secondary-phase inclusions. That fits expectation: the alpha crystal structure dissolves few impurities, so they precipitate out. The delta samples, stabilized and more soluble, showed fewer of them. A working lab matters beyond these samples. It is how plutonium work is verified and how aged material is judged. The report records the methods so the skill survives its builders.
doe-osti-3021668-grid-resiliency-using-h:
Joint Pacific Northwest and Idaho National Laboratory report PNNL-37324, by Sohom Datta and thirteen co-authors, dated August 2024, asks whether hydropower plants can anchor emergency microgrids when wildfires force power shutoffs. Utilities increasingly cut power on fire-prone days to avoid ignitions, leaving communities dark. A local hydro plant, already connected and staffed, could in principle island itself and keep critical loads running.

The team screened 740 hydropower plants across California, Oregon, Washington, and Idaho using the HydroSource database, sorting them by size, number of units, and operating mode. The screening feeds a hydropower resilience designation process that scores plants for microgrid duty. The report lays out the analysis steps and the plant characteristics that favor islanded operation, giving grid planners a method to find candidate sites before the next fire season.
his-dog:
Albert Payson Terhune gave his 1922 novel His Dog a hero ground down by dirt farming in the North Jersey hills. Link Ferris inherited forty worked-out acres, a mortgage, and a shack from his Civil War veteran father, and his life runs in a circle of labor, sleep, and hard cider. Into that barren routine comes a dog, and the four long chapters, The Derelict, The Battle, The Ordeal, and The Choice, turn on what the animal asks of him.

Terhune's derelict is the man, not the dog: the collie's devotion becomes the one claim on Link that the farm cannot make. The story is spare beside the Sunnybank books, a redemption tale in which a dog's faithfulness rebuilds a wasted life.
in-the-fog:
Richard Harding Davis set In the Fog at the Grill, a London club he calls the hardest in the world to enter. Members never name it, lest they seem to boast. The club blackballed a prime minister of each party, the tale claims. Four strangers at supper frame the mystery that follows.

A lost cigar-case and diamonds drive one inner tale. A man tears a dressing-case apart on a bed and finds nothing. Fog, club talk, and nested stories build the puzzle. Davis keeps the solution for the club room, in a tale of crime and wit.
lost-in-the-fog:
Lost in the Fog is a sea adventure for boys by James De Mille, dated 1870. It opens on a July morning on the wharf of Grand Pré. A crowd of schoolboys gathers there, old friends with names like Bruce, Arthur, Bart, and Tom. They are bound on a voyage aboard the Antelope, against the Doctor's warnings.

The boys are old acquaintances from Grand Pré School, and they talk like seasoned sailors. Their roundabout plan sets them on a highly eventful voyage. Fog, sea risk, and boyish daring drive the tale from the first chapter. De Mille writes with humor and a love of the Nova Scotia coast. It is a lively period piece of schoolboy adventure at sea.
navajo-weavers-third-annual-report-of-th:
Washington Matthews wrote Navajo Weavers for the third annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology, covering 1881 to 1882. The Government Printing Office issued it in Washington in 1884. Matthews served as a United States Army doctor. Plates show a woman spinning, a blanket loom, and belt weaving.

Figures lay out how warp threads run, how healds are set, and how saddle girths are woven. Other plates show finished blankets, some of the finest quality. Matthews also shows Zuni women weaving a belt for contrast. The piece records tools and steps in detail, so later readers can follow exactly how Navajo cloth was made.
our-friend-the-dog:
Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian author of The Life of the Bee, wrote Our Friend the Dog. The essay begins in grief. He has just lost Pelléas, a little bulldog of six months. The pup's knowing eyes opened to love mankind. They closed again on the cruel secrets of death. The name, he muses, could disgrace no man or hero. How can a poor dog be anything but loving, devoted, and faithful?

Pelléas had a bulging, powerful forehead, like Socrates or Verlaine. He had a smile Maeterlinck starts to describe. Then the essay turns from portrait to philosophy. In Alexander Teixeira de Mattos's translation it became a famous tribute. It asks what humans owe the one animal that chose them.
podcast-joerogan--s2d7cojsog:
Neuroscientist Andrew Huberman joins Joe Rogan for episode 1683 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Huberman is a Stanford professor whose own show made health steps a mass craze. His talks with Rogan are among the show's most saved.

Huberman lays out steps for sleep, light, focus, and strength that rest on lab work. He tells what he does at dawn, at work, and at night to keep his mind keen. Rogan tests the steps against his own hard routine. Listeners get a dense, useful talk. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated methods.
podcast-joerogan-zvqTC4nQkog:
Chef and TV star Matty Matheson tells Joe Rogan about growing up Mormon and being excommunicated in this clip. Matheson, known for loud humor and hit cooking shows, had a wild road from a strict faith to food fame. The story mixes church, family, and rebellion.

Matheson describes the rules and community of his Mormon youth with warmth and bite. He explains the break that led the church to cast him out and the rough years that followed. Rogan draws out the funny and painful parts in equal measure. Hungry and curious listeners get a meaty tale of faith lost and a life rebuilt.
the-adventures-of-grandfather-frog: For his Bedtime Story-Books, Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Grandfather Frog. Harrison Cady drew the plates. Little, Brown, and Company printed it at Boston in 1920. Chapters listed bring Billy Mink to the Smiling Pool first. Little Joe Otter joins him there. Longlegs the Blue Heron then pays a set of calls. Grandfather Frog's big mouth lands him in trouble. Spotty the Turtle plays doctor at the end.
the-camp-of-the-dog:
Algernon Blackwood opens The Camp of the Dog, dated 1908, with a voyage among islands. Past Stockholm the islands run north in their hundreds, of every shape and size. The little steamer that threads their intricate mazes in summer leaves the traveller bewildered as to the points of the compass by the time it reaches Waxholm. The tale is set in five parts, named by number alone.

After Waxholm, the narrator says, the true islands begin to run wild, up the coast in a tangled hundred-mile course of empty beauty. In the very heart of that confusion the party pitched their tents for a summer holiday. A wilderness of islands lay about them. Some lay so close that a strip of water no wider than a country lane ran between them.
the-day-of-the-dog: George Barr McCutcheon's The Day of the Dog was printed in New York in 1904, with pictures by Harrison Fisher and decorations by Margaret and Helen Maitland Armstrong. It is shown here only through its long list of illustrations. The captions name a dog called Swallow, a Mr. Crosby, Mrs. Delancy, Mrs. Austin, and Mr. Higgins, with scenes at a big red barn, a shallow brook, a theatre, and a place called Lonesomeville. Only the front matter and picture list are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-dog:
William Youatt's The Dog, edited with added notes by E. J. Lewis, is dated 1852 and was first entered in 1846. A list of plates names breed after breed. It runs from the southern hound and bloodhound to the Thibet dog and the dingo. It ends with the greyhound, the water spaniel, the poodle, and the Newfoundland. The English and Scotch sheep dogs close the roll.

Youatt was the age's chief voice on animal health. His book joins breed lore with care, training, and disease cures. Lewis, a Philadelphia doctor, adds notes for American readers. It stays a rich source on how the 1800s knew their dogs.
the-golden-dog:
William Kirby wrote The Golden Dog. It is also given as Le Chien d'Or. His prefatory note is signed at Niagara, Canada, in May 1897. The note tells the history of the book. A first edition came out in the United States in 1877. It came out without his knowledge. Weak copyright law let it go on selling in many editions. All profited but the author.

Kirby says L. C. Page and Company of Boston then stepped in. They asked him to revise the book. This revised edition is the only one with his sanction. He corrected it by the latest findings on the history of Quebec. The contents open with Men of the Old Regime. They name The Walls of Quebec and A Chatelaine of New France. They also name The Intendant Bigot. The tale is set in French Quebec under the old regime.
the-great-red-frog:
M. Yendis told and pictured The Great Red Frog. Methuen and Company printed it in London in 1903. Long ago, in a land far off, there lived a little Prince who looked just like the Lord Chamberlain's son. The likeness fooled even the sly old Chamberlain, who at times could not say which boy was which. The two grew up as playmates.

In time the Prince came to rule as King of Noware, and the pair still matched like two peas. One day, at play outdoors, a strange thing happened: a Magic Bush sprang up at the King's back. In that moment the Chamberlain's son lost his temper and shoved the King into the bush. The King came out a queer red Frog, and off it hopped, croaking in fright. The tale is a picture-book story for children. It is told page by page with the pictures.
the-under-dog:
F. Hopkinson Smith gathered his stories of life's losers in The Under Dog, published in 1903. A letter to readers opens the volume and sorts these figures into kinds. Some lose place through weakness or missed chances, some are misjudged by neighbours or crushed by the law, and some simply need sympathy to revive.

Smith says such people, grave and gay, have always appealed to him, and he prints their stories hoping readers will feel the same. The contents begin with a group called No Respecter of Persons. Its pieces include The Crime of Samanthy North, Bud Tilden the mail-thief, and a sentence measured out as eleven months and ten days.
the-voice-in-the-fog:
Harold MacGrath published The Voice in the Fog in 1915 with Grosset and Dunlap and the Bobbs-Merrill Company, illustrated by A. B. Wenzell. He dedicates the novel to Cav. Giovanni Piccinini, remembering happy Florentine days. A frontispiece names a character, Kitty Killigrew, before the story starts.

Chapter one is a single subject: fog. MacGrath renders a London fog as solid and substantial, yellow as an old dog's tooth or a jaundiced eye. Sight fails completely inside it, and only touch stays trustworthy, feeling the vapour's substance on the palms and through clothing. The opening withholds people and plot, letting weather itself become the mystery's first actor.
three-men-in-a-boat-to-say-nothing-of-th:
Jerome K. Jerome published Three Men in a Boat, to say nothing of the dog, at Bristol and London in 1889, with illustrations by A. Frederics. His preface claims the book's chief beauty is simple truthfulness. Its pages record events that really happened, only coloured a little at no extra charge.

George, Harris, and Montmorency are flesh and blood, he insists, especially George at about twelve stone. Other books may beat it in depth or originality, Jerome says, but none in incurable veracity. Readers get a Thames boating holiday turned into enduring comic travel writing.
tom-cringle-s-log:
Michael Scott, who lived from 1789 to 1835, narrates his naval log through Thomas Cringle, a boy dazzled by Trafalgar's glories. Cringle stands four feet four inches tall at thirteen and resolves that Britain needs a successor to Nelson. He torments every relative until their influence converges on an admiral.

A letter with a formidable seal then arrives at Sunday breakfast, and his mother weeps over it in silence. She pushes the manuscript toward him, covers her face, and leaves the room praying. Readers get a comic, sorrowful start to a sailor's career, launched by a child's ambition.
